questions.question: What does a position-time graph represent?
options: The physical path of the object in space
The object's position as a function of time
questions.answer: The object's position as a function of time
questions.explanation: The lecturer explicitly states that x is a function of time and the graph shows x versus t.
questions.flashcard_front: What does a position-time graph show?
questions.flashcard_back: It shows position as a function of time, not the physical path of the object.
questions.flashcard_explanation: The graph depicts x(t), meaning it tracks position over time, not the spatial trajectory.

questions.question: If an object's average velocity is zero, it must have remained stationary for the entire duration.
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains that an object could move and return to its starting position, resulting in an average velocity of zero.
questions.flashcard_front: Can average velocity be zero if an object moved?
questions.flashcard_back: Yes, if the object returns to its starting position, the displacement is zero.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Average velocity is displacement over time; zero displacement results in zero average velocity.

questions.question: How is instantaneous velocity represented on a position-time graph?
questions.answer: It is represented by the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that specific point.
questions.explanation: The lecturer defines instantaneous velocity as the derivative dx/dt, which corresponds to the tangent of the curve at a point.
questions.flashcard_front: What is instantaneous velocity on a position-time graph?
questions.flashcard_back: The slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point.
questions.flashcard_explanation: The derivative dx/dt represents the slope of the tangent at any given time t.

questions.question: Why is there no common name for the third derivative of position?
questions.answer: There are no physical equations that involve the third derivative explicitly.
questions.explanation: The lecturer notes that while you can take any number of derivatives, only the first two have names because they appear in fundamental laws like F=ma.
questions.flashcard_front: Why does the third derivative of position lack a name?
questions.flashcard_back: No physical equations explicitly involve the third derivative.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Only the first two derivatives (velocity and acceleration) are used in fundamental equations like F=ma.
